Any error occurring from test ordering and specimen collection up to the moment the sample enters the analyzer.
Contained in grey-top blood collection tubes alongside potassium oxalate.
Prevents erythrocytes from consuming glucose at 5% to 7% per hour after venepuncture.
An antiglycolytic preservative that inhibits the glycolytic enzyme enolase for accurate plasma glucose measurement.
Should be suspected when a markedly elevated potassium result occurs with a normal ECG and no clinical symptoms.
Can result from fist clenching, in vitro haemolysis, thrombocytosis, or refrigerating unseparated whole blood.
An artifactual elevation of serum potassium released from cells after blood collection without true in vivo hyperkalaemia.
Forms the quantitative physical foundation of clinical spectrophotometry.

Principle stating that light absorbance is directly proportional to chromogen concentration and optical path length.
Classically encountered with massively elevated serum beta-hCG, prolactin, or ferritin levels.
Resolved by repeating the immunoassay after serial dilution of the patient's serum.

Evaluated daily using Westgard multi-rules such as 1_3s, 2_2s, and 10_x.

A graphical plot of sequential internal quality control results over time used to monitor analytical precision and bias.

terms.sub: Reference Values and Diagnostic Test Evaluation
clues: By statistical convention, 5% of healthy individuals fall outside its upper and lower limits.
Preferred modern terminology over 'normal range' because values vary with age, sex, and population.
The central 95% distribution of laboratory test values derived from a well-defined healthy population.

terms.sub: Reference Values and Diagnostic Test Evaluation
clues: Calculated as True Positives divided by the sum of True Positives plus False Negatives.
A test with a very high value for this metric is ideal for ruling out disease when negative (SnNout).
The probability that a diagnostic test yields a positive result in a patient who truly has the target disease.

terms.sub: Reference Values and Diagnostic Test Evaluation
clues: Unlike sensitivity and specificity, this metric rises and falls strongly with disease prevalence.
Calculated as True Positives divided by all positive test results (TP + FP).
The probability that a patient who receives a positive test result actually has the disease.

terms.sub: Post-analytical Phase, Critical Values, and Point-of-Care Testing
clues: Particularly effective for catching 'wrong blood in tube' specimen labelling errors.
Automated post-analytical algorithm comparing consecutive results from the same patient.
A quality verification rule that flags an implausibly large change between a patient's current result and their previous result.
